title: When Aspirations Don't Line Up With Skill
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note tackles a specific and difficult leadership problem: team members whose career aspirations vastly outpace their actual skills, compounded by low self-awareness that makes direct feedback nearly useless. The author argues that a frontal assault — simply telling the person the hard truth — tends to produce either explosive resistance or collapse, because a person who lacked the self-awareness to see the gap on their own is unlikely to accept it from a single voice, even the leader's. The recommended alternative is to gather structured, qualitative feedback from multiple colleagues and let the sheer weight of consistent outside perception do the convincing, with the leader positioned as the compassionate messenger rather than the sole judge. The piece frames this multi-voice approach as protecting the leader-employee relationship even as it delivers unwelcome news, and closes by reframing the whole exercise as a gift, however unwelcome it may initially feel to the recipient.
points: Team members with low self-awareness are, by definition, unlikely to accept a leader's single, direct assessment that their skills don't match their aspirations.
A frontal, one-on-one confrontation about a skill-aspiration gap tends to produce either fireworks or surrender rather than genuine understanding.
Collecting structured, qualitative feedback from multiple colleagues and presenting it together makes the gap harder to dismiss than any single leader's opinion.
Using outside voices to deliver the hard truth protects the leader-employee relationship, since the team member doesn't reject the leader along with the message.
quotes: Colleagues with low self-awareness are also commonly blind to how others see and judge them and their skills.
Convincing a colleague with low self-awareness that they do not have the skills or talents to achieve their aspirations is nearly impossible.
Good leaders don't make a frontal assault on this gap when they are dealing with an unaware team member.
Leaders collect the perceptions of others and then allow the unaware team member to stare reality in the eye and accept or reject it.
Even for those without self-awareness, just seeing how a large swath of colleagues perceives them becomes irrefutable.
Changing the awareness of those without it is a herculean task. The first step toward this change is understanding.
